standard.title: Diversity of First Nations dance
standard.description: investigate the diversity of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have diverse dance traditions. They have not yet investigated this diversity systematically or engaged with ICIP rights frameworks in dance contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian dance with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights in dance contexts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights mean in dance contexts and describe what culturally responsive engagement with First Nations dance looks like in practice
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what ICIP rights are in a dance context; give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations dance looks like
nodes.typical_width: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to dance practice — using movement vocabulary, performing First Nations dances, referencing choreographic approaches
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in dance where ICIP rights were denied — explain what happened, who was harmed, and what a respectful alternative would have been
Research the questions practitioners should ask when engaging with First Nations dance material — 'Who created this dance?', 'Who owns these movements?' — and develop own practical guidelines
Explore how ICIP rights in dance differ from copyright in other arts — analyse why collective ownership of movement vocabulary requires different protocols

response_modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights in the abstract without being able to reason through specific dance scenarios — they know 'you need permission' without knowing who to ask, what counts as cultural movement vocabulary, or what respectful engagement looks like in practice. Scaffolding scenario-based reasoning builds actionable understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The cultural appropriation case study direction is genuinely rich — it requires reasoning about harm, rights and alternatives in a concrete case. The collective ownership direction also opens important conceptual territory: why movement vocabulary that belongs to a community requires fundamentally different protocols than individual artistic copyright.
success_criteria: Explains what ICIP rights mean in a dance context
Gives at least one specific example of respectful engagement
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind protocols

nodes.label: Investigating diversity of First Nations Australian dance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian dance practices across regions and contexts with cultural responsiveness
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian dance work or choreographer in depth; explain what makes it culturally significant
nodes.typical_width: Investigate First Nations Australian dance from at least two different regional or cultural contexts; analyse what is distinctive about each and how ICIP responsibilities apply
wider: Use a map of First Nations Australian language groups to identify where choreographers and performers are working — investigate the geographic and cultural breadth of First Nations dance practice
Analyse how linear and non-linear narrative is used in specific First Nations Australian dance works to explore issues of identity, relationships or empathy
Investigate a contemporary First Nations Australian choreographer working in contemporary or cross-cultural contexts — analyse how they navigate cultural identity and ICIP responsibilities

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian dance as a single tradition rather than understanding the enormous diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups, regions, and contemporary/traditional contexts. Multiple distinct investigation contexts — different regions, contemporary vs traditional, cross-cultural — resolve this misconception through genuine breadth.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The geographic mapping direction and the narrative analysis direction both give advancing students genuine analytical depth. The contemporary First Nations choreographer direction is particularly rich — it surfaces how artists navigate identity and ICIP responsibilities in contemporary global dance contexts.
success_criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian dance or practice in genuine depth
Explains cultural significance — not just describes what the dance looks like

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make ethical choices about how they engage with First Nations Australian dance, applying ICIP protocols to their own practice as audience members, students and performers.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own dance practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
nodes.typical_width: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian dance in learning and performance contexts.
wider: Evaluate a specific case of cultural appropriation in dance — analyse who was harmed, what rights were denied, and what a respectful alternative would have been.
Develop personal guidelines for culturally responsive engagement with First Nations Australian dance, grounded in specific protocols.
success_criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical dance practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

response_modes.reason: Applying protocols requires reasoning through specific dance contexts — who created this movement, whose story is it, what permission is needed.
